impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. This ruling forecloses plaintiffs from relying on the pendency of a class action to toll the statute of limitations for individual claims filed in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides finality and predictability for the government and entities facing potential class-related litigation in the Court of Federal Claims, reducing the risk of stale individual claims being revived after class action tolling.
impacts.negativeImplications: Investors and businesses pursuing takings or breach of contract claims against the government must independently monitor and meet the six-year deadline, as participation in a related class action will not toll the limitations period.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of Federal Claims erred in its methodology for assessing copyright infringement damages, including whether an existing license agreement compels the damages framework and whether the court improperly applied the 'book of wisdom' doctrine to award non-compensatory damages against the government.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright damages rather than deferring to the terms of an existing license, but vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages. This case provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government infringement cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms flexibility in damages methodology, allowing courts to assess copyright damages via hypothetical negotiation even when an existing license exists, which can benefit copyright holders seeking higher valuations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Limits the ability of copyright holders to recover non-compensatory or punitive-style damages against the government, and clarifies that post-infringement evidence under the 'book of wisdom' doctrine cannot be used to inflate damages beyond actual compensation.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations for a Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) claim had expired before Insulet brought suit, given evidence that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages award in favor of Insulet, holding that EOFlow was entitled to judgment as a matter of law because the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the alleged trade secret misappropriation well before the limitations period began. This is a significant ruling on DTSA limitations and the discovery rule.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides strong statute-of-limitations defense for companies accused of trade secret misappropriation when the plaintiff had constructive or actual knowledge of the alleged misappropriation beyond the three-year window.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon learning or having reason to know of potential misappropriation; delay in filing suit, even while investigating, risks forfeiting DTSA claims entirely.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and its chosen damages methodology, and whether the jury's breach of contract damages award should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the breach of contract judgment and reinstated the jury award. The decision affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law. This case significantly impacts how damages are measured in trade secret misappropriation cases involving software licensing relationships.
impacts.positiveImplications: Broadens the range of acceptable damages models for trade secret misappropriation, potentially allowing plaintiffs to pursue unjust enrichment and other previously excluded theories. Reinstates a jury's breach of contract award, supporting the sanctity of jury findings on contract damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face increased exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims with potentially broader damages theories, including enrichment-based measures.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form containing a single infringement question covering multiple patents, and a flawed jury instruction on patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, required vacatur of the infringement and damages judgments.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's single question covering infringement of all asserted patents was impermissibly ambiguous, and that further proceedings were needed under Alice step two for the § 101 analysis. The court affirmed that two of the patents survived § 101 challenges at step one.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that building automation system patents directed to wireless communication improvements are not necessarily abstract ideas under § 101, preserving patent value for IoT and smart home technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders must ensure verdict forms separately address infringement for each asserted patent; combined questions risk vacatur of otherwise substantial jury awards. This increases trial complexity and cost.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent's claims were entitled to claim priority from a provisional application where the patent changed a chemical substituent range (C2-C12 to C1-C12), allegedly to correct a typographical error, and whether intervening prior art anticipated the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that Enanta's '953 patent could not claim priority from its provisional application because the change from C2 to C1 in a chemical substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error. Without the earlier priority date, Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid) anticipated the patent's claims. This ruling has major implications for pharmaceutical patent drafting and provisional application practice.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from a strict standard for correcting alleged typographical errors in provisional applications, reducing the risk that competitors can retroactively expand patent scope.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies face severe consequences from even minor errors in provisional applications; seemingly small typographical mistakes can forfeit an earlier priority date and render patents invalid due to intervening prior art.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting two invalidity grounds that were not included in a prior IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The decision refines the standard for determining what prior art a 'skilled searcher conducting a diligent search' reasonably could have been expected to discover for purposes of § 315(e)(2) estoppel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides accused infringers with greater latitude to raise invalidity defenses in district court that were not included in prior IPR petitions, narrowing the scope of IPR estoppel and preserving litigation options.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face reduced ability to leverage IPR estoppel to eliminate invalidity defenses at trial, potentially increasing the cost and complexity of enforcing patents after IPR proceedings.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101 but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, suggesting that the pursuit of clearly ineligible claims may warrant attorney fee awards. This case reinforces the vulnerability of data collection and processing claims in agricultural technology to § 101 challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Ag-tech and IoT companies accused of infringing data-collection patents gain a stronger basis for invalidity challenges under § 101, and may recover attorney fees in exceptional cases involving weak patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on precision agriculture systems, IoT data collection, and similar technologies face heightened § 101 invalidity risk, and aggressive enforcement of such patents may lead to exceptional case findings and fee-shifting.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement possesses sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains an exclusionary right—specifically the right to sue third parties for infringement—has the irreducible constitutional minimum of standing, even after granting an exclusive license. This clarifies that retaining enforcement rights is sufficient for Article III standing in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain enforcement rights and independently bring infringement actions, providing flexibility in monetization strategies and ensuring access to courts even after licensing core commercial rights.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot easily challenge standing based on the existence of an exclusive license when the patent owner has expressly retained the right to sue, potentially increasing the number of parties that can bring infringement actions.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent and whether it permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic drug from entering the market before patent expiration, upholding the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that the equities did not support complete waiver pending appeal. This decision is significant for Hatch-Waxman litigation and the standard for bond requirements in pharmaceutical patent injunctions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies can secure preliminary injunctions to block generic market entry during patent litigation, protecting market exclusivity through patent expiration.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic manufacturers may be blocked from market entry by preliminary injunctions, but the requirement of a bond pending appeal provides some financial protection; brand companies cannot avoid posting security merely by asserting strong equities.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of UT's drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implant patent used in drug-eluting coronary stents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's infringement verdict in favor of UT, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on both invalidity (anticipation) and non-infringement of claims directed to drug-releasing biodegradable polymer fiber compositions used in coronary stents. The court also mooted UT's cross-appeal on willfulness. This decision eliminates a significant patent assertion against a major medical device product line.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from a rigorous application of anticipation and non-infringement standards, protecting established product lines like drug-eluting stents from overbroad patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and licensees face heightened risk of JMOL reversal of jury verdicts, particularly where prior art closely aligns with the claimed invention.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds based on a prior IPR decision against related claims, and whether it erred in awarding attorney fees under § 285 and sanctions under § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the surviving patent claims invalid on the same obviousness grounds applied in an IPR to related claims. However, the court reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and § 1927 attorney sanctions, holding that the grounds presented were insufficient to support those determinations. This clarifies the threshold for fee-shifting in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can leverage IPR invalidity findings against related claims to defeat infringement complaints at the pleading stage. The reversal of fee sanctions provides some comfort to patent plaintiffs that aggressive but non-frivolous enforcement will not automatically trigger penalties.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders whose claims survive IPR may still face dismissal if related claims were invalidated on grounds equally applicable to surviving claims, limiting the value of partial IPR victories.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents should be measured at a standard temperature recognized in the field, and whether infringement by equivalents was properly barred.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed non-infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, holding that 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at the standard temperature in the field (25°C). The court also upheld the finding that Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. This provides important guidance on how temperature-dependent claim terms in pharmaceutical patents should be interpreted.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from a clear standard for interpreting temperature-dependent claim limitations, providing certainty in designing around branded pharmaceutical patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies may find it more difficult to capture generic formulations under claims with pH or other condition-dependent limitations if the standard measurement conditions are narrowly defined.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions should be treated as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of the intervening Dyfan v. Target precedent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration under the Dyfan framework, which issued after the district court's original ruling. The court held that further analysis was needed to determine whether 'executable program code configured to' invokes § 112(f) means-plus-function treatment. The court affirmed invalidity of the '638 patent for anticipation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders may benefit from the Dyfan framework, which could prevent certain software claim terms from being automatically treated as means-plus-function limitations, potentially saving claims from indefiniteness invalidation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent assertions face continued uncertainty about when software claim terms will be subject to § 112(f), complicating invalidity defenses.

impacts.caseName: Wyeth LLC v. AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether asserted claims directed to methods of treating gefitinib/erlotinib-resistant non-small cell lung cancer with irreversible EGFR inhibitors were invalid as a matter of law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed JMOL of invalidity of Wyeth's cancer treatment method patents, which claimed use of irreversible EGFR inhibitors for treating drug-resistant NSCLC. This decision removes a significant patent assertion in the oncology therapeutic space and provides guidance on the evidentiary standards for upholding invalidity determinations as a matter of law in pharmaceutical method-of-treatment cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies developing competing cancer therapies, including irreversible EGFR inhibitors, can do so without risk of infringement of these specific Wyeth patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the pharmaceutical method-of-treatment space face heightened risk of JMOL invalidity where the claimed methods build upon well-known therapeutic approaches.
